I served 21 years in the Marine Corps as an infantry officer with 3 years in combat.

If the enemy is wearing a uniform then the rules are pretty clear. The Geneva Convention clearly applies.

But if the enemy is wearing civilian cloths, then the rules become much more difficult to follow.

I was a platoon commander in Vietnam. I was also an adviser in a Latin American country during a civil war for two years. I can tell you that you have no idea who the enemy is until you can positively identifying him/her shooting at you. That, my friend is very difficult.

So, you want to know who gave the order? Let's talk about who gave the order for the rules of engagement I had to follow.

  1. While on patrol in Vietnam, we could not have a magazine in our weapon or a round in our magazine until we could positively identify the enemy (who were dressed as civilians). In an ambush there is no time to put a magazine in your weapon and charge a round to begin returning fire--you would already be dead.

  2. We were required to wear a helmet and flak jacket on combat patrols at night. Both were impediments to patrolling quietly. To not have a helmet and flak jacket was a court martial offense. Did we wear helmets and flak jackets? Sometimes, but when it was a very risky mission, we did not. Did any of my Marines ever turn me in for violating the rules of engagement? No. Why? Because they knew as their platoon commander that I valued their lives more than my career or going to a court martial.

The orders you follow at the logical ones. You don't kill your enemy if he/she has obviously surrendered. You don't kill civilians if you can possibly avoid it. Etc.

But on the other hand, you don't follow orders that will get you and your unit killed. It's a two way street.

I believe most of the rules of engagement are written by lawyers who have never been in combat and have no idea of the consequences of their legal perspective in combat.

I followed the rules of engagement that made sense. I ignored the ones that would get me and my Marines killed.
